{{Short description|Irish mathematician}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Henry Gordon Dawson''' (2 August 1862 in [[Omagh|Omagh, County Tyrone]]{{spaced ndash}}22 February 1918 in [[Hastings]], [[East Sussex]]) was an Irish mathematician.  The [[Dawson function]] is named after him.<ref>[http://mathworld.wolfram.com/DawsonsIntegral.html Dawson's Integral] [[Mathworld]]</ref>

==Education and career==
Dawson was educated at [[Trinity College Dublin]] (BA 1882, 1st Senior Moderator and Gold Medallist)<ref>[https://books.google.com/books?id=yAwOAAAAYAAJ&dq=%22+Dawson%2C+Henry+Gordon%22&pg=PA61 A Catalogue of Graduates of the University of Dublin], Volume 2</ref> and at [[Christ's College, Cambridge]] (BA as 19th wrangler 1886, MA 1890).  In 1897 he created the function that has since been named after him.<ref>{{cite journal | author = Dawson, H. G. | title = On the Numerical Value of <math>\int_0^h \exp(x^2) \, dx</math>| volume = s1-29 | number = 1 | pages = 519–522 | year = 1897 | doi=10.1112/plms/s1-29.1.519| journal = Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society | url = https://zenodo.org/record/1433401}}</ref> His career included stints as Mathematical Lecturer at Cambridge (at least 1888–94) and at [[Firth College, Sheffield]] (1901–10). He was a member of the [[Royal Irish Academy]].<ref name=yearbook>[https://archive.org/stream/oxfordcambridge01hollgoog/oxfordcambridge01hollgoog_djvu.txt Dawson, Henry Gordon] Digital copy of full text of "The Oxford & Cambridge Yearbook ..."</ref>
